ask_the_logic.question: If score is 45 and the check is 'if score >= 50:', does Python crash, skip the indented block, or print an error?
options: It skips the indented block silently and moves on to the code after it.
ask_the_logic.explanation: When an if condition evaluates to False, Python skips the indented block entirely and continues running whatever code comes afterwards.

cards.title: Passing or Failing an Exam
cards.text: You already know how variables store numbers. But a college grading system cannot treat every student the same way. If a student scores 75, we must print 'Pass'. If they score 30, we must print 'Retry'. Without decision making, code runs blindly from top to bottom.

cards.title: An if Statement is a Fork in the Road
cards.text: An if statement checks a true-or-false condition like a toll gate: if the condition is True, code enters the gate; if False, the gate stays closed and code skips past.

cards.title: Smallest Valid Syntax Labelled
cards.text: The colon (:) at the end of the line signals a block. Indentation (4 spaces) defines what code belongs inside the condition.
cards.code:
if score >= 50:
    print("Pass!")
# 1. 'if' keyword
# 2. Condition (score >= 50) evaluates to True or False
# 3. Colon ':' mandatory
# 4. Indented body (4 spaces) executes ONLY if True

cards.title: Side-by-Side: Checking Pass Mark
cards.text: Plan the decision logic in plain words before writing the Python statement.
logic_plan: 2. Check if score is at least 50.
cards.code:
score = 75
if score >= 50:
    print("Pass!")
print("Evaluation complete")

cards.title: Step-by-Step Visualizer & Trace Table
cards.text: Step through execution and watch the trace table check the condition.

steps.explanation: Line 2: 75 >= 50 evaluates to True. Python enters the indented block.

cards.title: Decision Flowchart
cards.text: The diamond represents the condition split.

cards.title: Predict First, Then Try
cards.text: What if score is changed to 40? Predict before running: 40 >= 50 evaluates to False. Line 3 is skipped completely, so only 'Evaluation complete' is printed!
cards.code:
score = 40
if score >= 50:
    print("Pass!")
print("Evaluation complete")

cards.title: Using '=' Instead of '==' for Comparison
cards.text: Mistake: Writing if score = 50: instead of ==. Single '=' assigns a value. Double '==' checks equality. Python raises a SyntaxError to protect you.
cards.code:
# WRONG:
# if score = 50:  # SyntaxError: invalid syntax

# FIXED:
score = 50
if score == 50:
    print("Exact pass mark!")

cards.title: Test Your Understanding
cards.text: Check your grasp of conditions and comparison operators.

questions.q: Which operator checks if two numbers are NOT equal in Python?
questions.why: != is the not-equal comparison operator in Python.

questions.q: What happens if you omit the colon ':' at the end of an if line?
questions.why: The colon ':' is required syntax to tell Python that an indented code block follows.

cards.title: Skill Earned!
cards.text: You can now form boolean comparison conditions and control program flow with if statements.

ask_the_logic.question: In an if-elif-else chain, if the first 'if' condition is True, does Python evaluate the 'elif' condition below it?
options: No, once any branch in an if-elif chain is True, all subsequent elif and else branches are skipped.
Yes, Python always evaluates every elif in the file.
Only if the score is greater than 100.
ask_the_logic.explanation: An if-elif-else ladder is mutually exclusive. The very first branch that matches runs, and the rest are skipped immediately.

cards.title: More Than Just Two Options
cards.text: You already know how if handles one check. But letter grades have many tiers: A (>=90), B (>=75), C (>=50), and F (below 50). Writing separate if statements is messy and redundant. We need clean multi-way branching.

cards.title: An if-elif-else Chain is an Ordered Priority Ladder
cards.text: Python tests branches from top to bottom. As soon as one condition matches, its block runs, and Python jumps past the entire rest of the chain.

cards.title: The elif-else Syntax Rules
cards.text: 'elif' means 'else if'. You can have zero or many elif blocks. 'else' has no condition and acts as the catch-all safety net.

cards.title: Side-by-Side: Assigning Grades
cards.text: Structure conditions from most restrictive to least restrictive.
logic_plan: 3. Else if marks >= 75: Grade is B.

cards.title: Step-by-Step Visualizer & Trace Table
cards.text: Watch Python skip the remaining branches once a match is found.

steps.explanation: Assign 'grade' = 'B'. Now skip past 'else' to line 7!

cards.title: Grade Decision Tree
cards.text: Shows how code branches and exits cleanly.

cards.title: Predict First, Then Try
cards.text: What if marks is 95? Predict: 95 >= 90 is True on the very first line! 'grade' becomes 'A', and Python skips the elif entirely even though 95 is ALSO >= 75.

cards.title: Wrong Condition Ordering
cards.text: Mistake: Putting if marks >= 50 first before marks >= 90. Because 95 is >= 50, the first check catches it and gives grade C instead of A! Always check most specific condition first.
cards.code:
# WRONG:
# if marks >= 50: grade = 'C' # 95 gets caught here!
# elif marks >= 90: grade = 'A'

# FIXED: Order from highest threshold down to lowest

cards.title: Test Your Understanding
cards.text: Verify your mental model of branch execution.

questions.q: Can you have an 'else' block without an 'if' block?
options: No, else must always be paired with a preceding if
questions.why: Every else block must belong to a preceding if statement.

questions.q: How many branches in an if-elif-else ladder can execute?
questions.why: In any if-elif-else chain, at most ONE block ever runs.

cards.title: Skill Earned!
cards.text: You can now structure mutually exclusive if-elif-else ladders with proper condition ordering.

title: Combining Logic: and, or, not
badge_skill: Combines conditions with and, or, and not

ask_the_logic.question: If condition A is False, does Python even check condition B in 'if A and B:'?
options: No, this is called short-circuit evaluation: if the left of 'and' is False, the whole thing is already False.
Yes, Python always evaluates both sides no matter what.
ask_the_logic.explanation: Python uses short-circuit evaluation. For 'and', if the first part is False, the whole condition cannot possibly be True, so Python skips evaluating the second part.

cards.title: Checking Multiple Conditions at Once
cards.text: You already know how to test a single condition like score >= 50. But real-world rules require multiple criteria: for campus placements, a student needs CGPA >= 7.5 AND attendance >= 75%. Testing these with nested if statements gets ugly fast.

cards.title: Logical Operators Glue Conditions Together
cards.text: 'and' requires BOTH sides to be True. 'or' requires AT LEAST ONE side to be True. 'not' flips True to False and False to True.
cards.code:
cgpa = 8.2
attendance = 80
if cgpa >= 7.5 and attendance >= 75:
    print("Eligible for interview!")

cards.title: Truth Tables in Code
cards.text: Remember: True and False is False. True or False is True. not True is False.
cards.code:
A and B -> True ONLY when both A and B are True
A or B  -> True if either A is True, B is True, or both
not A   -> Reverses boolean (not False == True)

cards.title: Side-by-Side: Placement Eligibility
cards.text: Express the compound requirement cleanly.
logic_plan: 1. Record student cgpa as 8.2 and attendance as 80.
2. Check if cgpa is >= 7.5 AND attendance >= 75.

cards.title: Step-by-Step Visualizer & Trace Table
cards.text: Trace both parts of the compound condition.

steps.explanation: Check: 8.2 >= 7.5 (True) AND 80 >= 75 (True). Both True -> Enter block!

cards.title: Compound Decision Diagram
cards.text: Visualizing how AND demands both gates to open.

cards.title: Predict First, Then Try
cards.text: What if we replace 'and' with 'or' and set attendance = 60? Predict: 8.2 >= 7.5 is True. Because it is 'or', one True is enough, so it STILL prints 'Eligible!'!
cards.code:
cgpa = 8.2
attendance = 60
if cgpa >= 7.5 or attendance >= 75:
    print("Eligible via OR!")

cards.title: Writing 'if x == 1 or 2:'
cards.text: Mistake: Writing if x == 1 or 2:. Python evaluates (x == 1) or (2). Since 2 is a non-zero number, it is always truthy, so the condition is ALWAYS True regardless of x! Write if x == 1 or x == 2: instead.
cards.code:
# WRONG:
# if x == 1 or 2:  # Always True!

# FIXED:
x = 5
if x == 1 or x == 2:
    print("Matched!")

cards.title: Test Your Understanding
cards.text: Test your compound logic reasoning.

questions.q: What is the result of: not (5 > 2)?
questions.why: 5 > 2 is True. not True inverts it to False.

questions.q: What does True or False evaluate to?
questions.why: With the 'or' operator, if at least one operand is True, the result is True.

cards.title: Skill Earned!
cards.text: You can now combine complex requirements using and, or, and not with short-circuit awareness.
